about: 1P1 Mechanics is the first engineering mechanics course in Part IA of the Cambridge Engineering Tripos, given in 2025-26 as 16 lectures (two a week) in weeks 1-8 of Michaelmas Term. Following the official syllabus, it moves from Newton's laws and free-body diagrams through particle kinematics and dynamics (energy, momentum, variable mass, angular momentum and satellite orbits) to the kinematics and dynamics of rigid bodies in plane motion, including moments of inertia and impact. It is examined in Part IA Paper 1 (Mechanical Engineering), a 3-hour paper (per the 2025-26 Part IA guide) shared with Mechanical Vibrations and Thermofluid Mechanics. Topics and order follow the 2025-26 course page; check the 2026-27 page and Moodle for any changes.

notes.h: Newton's laws, units, forces and free-body diagrams
notes.body:
The course opens by fixing the ground rules that every later problem depends on. Most marks lost in Part IA mechanics come from a wrong or incomplete free-body diagram, not from hard algebra.

Newton's laws
- First law: a particle stays at rest or moves with constant velocity unless a net force acts on it.
- Second law: the net force equals the rate of change of linear momentum, F = d(mv)/dt. For constant mass this is F = ma.
- Third law: when body A pushes on body B, B pushes back on A with an equal and opposite force along the same line.

Units and dimensions
- SI base units for mechanics are the kilogram, metre and second. The newton is the force that gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s², so 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻².
- Check every answer for dimensional consistency. For example, √(k/m) with k in N/m and m in kg has units s⁻¹, so it can be a frequency in rad/s; √(m/k) cannot.

Common forces
- Weight mg acting at the centre of mass (g ≈ 9.81 m/s² near the Earth's surface).
- Normal reaction N, perpendicular to a contact surface.
- Coulomb friction F, tangential to the surface: F ≤ μN when there is no slip, and F = μN opposing the relative sliding when slip occurs.
- Spring force kx (linear spring of stiffness k extended by x), string tension, and viscous damping force cv.

Free-body diagrams
- Isolate one body (or a chosen system), draw it alone, and mark every external force on it with a clear direction.
- Do not include internal forces between parts of the chosen system, and do not draw "ma" as a force unless you are deliberately using d'Alembert's method.
- Choose axes that make the geometry simple (for an incline, along and normal to the slope).

Frames of reference
- Newton's laws hold in an inertial frame. Any frame moving with constant velocity relative to an inertial frame is also inertial.
- A frame fixed to the Earth is close enough to inertial for most engineering problems. Frames that accelerate or rotate (a braking car, a turntable) are not inertial, and Newton's second law then needs extra terms.

Worked example
A 2 kg block slides down a rough plane inclined at 30° with μ = 0.2. Normal to the slope: N = mg cos 30° = 16.99 N. Along the slope: mg sin 30° − μN = ma, so a = g(sin 30° − μ cos 30°) = 9.81 × (0.5 − 0.1732) = 3.21 m/s².

Exam tips: always draw the free-body diagram first, state your sign convention, and check units and limiting cases (for example μ = 0) before moving on.

notes.h: Particle kinematics in three coordinate systems
notes.body:
Kinematics describes motion without asking what causes it. The skill tested is choosing the coordinate system that suits the geometry and differentiating correctly, remembering that some unit vectors rotate.

Cartesian coordinates
- r = x i + y j, v = ẋ i + ẏ j, a = ẍ i + ÿ j.
- The unit vectors i and j are fixed, so differentiation is component by component. Best for projectiles and straight-line guides.

Polar coordinates
- r = r e_r, where e_r points away from the origin and e_θ is at 90° to it in the direction of increasing θ.
- These unit vectors turn as the particle moves: de_r/dt = θ̇ e_θ and de_θ/dt = −θ̇ e_r.
- Differentiating gives v = ṙ e_r + rθ̇ e_θ.
- Differentiating again gives a = (r̈ − rθ̇²) e_r + (rθ̈ + 2ṙθ̇) e_θ.
- −rθ̇² is the centripetal term; 2ṙθ̇ is the Coriolis term, which appears whenever r and θ change together (a bead sliding along a rotating rod).
- Best for anything rotating about a fixed point: arms, slots, orbits.

Intrinsic (path) coordinates
- e_t is tangent to the path in the direction of motion; e_n is normal to the path, pointing towards the centre of curvature.
- v = v e_t and a = v̇ e_t + (v²/ρ) e_n, where ρ is the local radius of curvature.
- Best when the path is known (a road, a track) and you care about speed changes and cornering.
- Example: a car at 20 m/s on a bend of radius 50 m, braking at 3 m/s². Normal acceleration = 20²/50 = 8 m/s², tangential = 3 m/s² (opposing motion), so |a| = √(8² + 3²) = 8.54 m/s².

Relative motion
- For two particles A and B, r_B = r_A + r_B/A. Differentiating: v_B = v_A + v_B/A and a_B = a_A + a_B/A.
- These simple forms hold when the relative quantities are measured in a frame that translates but does not rotate. Rotating frames are treated later with rigid bodies.

Numerical differentiation
- Measured positions are often sampled at time step Δt. A central difference estimates v_n ≈ (x_{n+1} − x_{n−1})/(2Δt) and a_n ≈ (x_{n+1} − 2x_n + x_{n−1})/Δt².
- Differentiation amplifies measurement noise, especially for acceleration, so smoothing or a sensible Δt matters.

Exam tips: write the polar acceleration from memory but be ready to derive it from the unit-vector derivatives; always check which way e_n points and include both acceleration components when finding a total.

notes.h: Equations of motion, d'Alembert force and numerical solution
notes.body:
Once forces and kinematics are in hand, Newton's second law gives the equations of motion. Many Part IA questions ask you to set these up carefully and then either solve them exactly or say how you would solve them numerically.

Setting up equations of motion
- Draw the free-body diagram.
- Write the acceleration in the coordinate system that matches the geometry (Cartesian, polar or intrinsic).
- Apply F = ma in each direction. Unknown constraint forces (normal reactions, tensions) usually come out of one component; the motion comes from another.

d'Alembert's principle
- Rewrite F = ma as F + (−ma) = 0. The term −ma is treated as an extra "inertia force" (the d'Alembert force) acting on the body.
- The dynamics problem then looks like a statics problem: forces including the d'Alembert force sum to zero, and so do their moments. This is especially convenient when taking moments about a point other than the centre of mass.
- The d'Alembert force is not a real interaction; it must never also appear alongside ma in the same equation.

Worked example: bead on a rotating rod
A smooth rod rotates in a horizontal plane at constant angular velocity ω about a vertical axis through O. A bead of mass m is released at radius r₀ with no radial velocity.
- Radial: there is no radial force on a smooth rod, so m(r̈ − rω²) = 0, giving r̈ = ω²r.
- The solution with r = r₀ and ṙ = 0 at t = 0 is r = r₀ cosh ωt.
- Transverse: N = m(rθ̈ + 2ṙθ̇) = 2mωṙ = 2mω²r₀ sinh ωt, the horizontal force the rod exerts on the bead. It grows rapidly because of the Coriolis term.

Numerical solution
- Most real equations of motion cannot be solved in closed form. Write the second-order equation as two first-order equations: ẋ = v and v̇ = a(x, v, t).
- Forward (explicit) Euler steps forward with x_{n+1} = x_n + v_n Δt and v_{n+1} = v_n + a_n Δt. It is simple but its error per unit time is proportional to Δt, and for undamped oscillators it slowly adds energy.
- Better schemes (semi-implicit Euler, Runge–Kutta) or a library ODE solver are used in practice; the course's reading includes a Python-based mechanics text.
- Always check a numerical answer by halving Δt and confirming the result hardly changes, and by testing a case with a known exact solution.

Example: with a = −x, x₀ = 0, v₀ = 1 and Δt = 0.1, two Euler steps give x₁ = 0.1, v₁ = 1, then x₂ = 0.2, v₂ = 0.99.

Exam tips: state which forces are known and which are unknown before writing equations, and check that the number of equations matches the number of unknowns.

notes.h: Work, energy, potential energy and stability
notes.body:
Energy methods replace vector equations with a single scalar equation. They are fastest when you need a speed at a position rather than an acceleration at an instant.

Work and kinetic energy
- The work done by a force F moving through a displacement is W = ∫ F · dr. Only the component of force along the motion does work.
- Kinetic energy of a particle is T = ½mv².
- The work–energy principle: the total work done on a particle equals its change in kinetic energy.
- Power is the rate of doing work, P = F · v.

Conservative forces and potential energy
- A force is conservative if the work it does depends only on the start and end positions. Then it can be written as F = −dV/dx in one dimension (F = −∇V in general).
- Uniform gravity: V = mgh. Linear spring: V = ½kx². Inverse-square gravity: V = −GMm/r.
- If only conservative forces do work, T + V is constant. Friction and damping remove mechanical energy, so then T + V falls by the energy dissipated.
- Normal reactions on smooth fixed surfaces do no work, which is why energy methods work so well for smooth tracks.

Equilibrium and stability
- For a system described by one coordinate q, equilibrium positions are where dV/dq = 0.
- Stable equilibrium: d²V/dq² > 0 (a minimum of V). Unstable: d²V/dq² < 0 (a maximum). If the second derivative is zero, look at higher derivatives.
- Example: a simple pendulum has V = −mgl cos θ. dV/dθ = mgl sin θ = 0 at θ = 0 and π. d²V/dθ² = mgl cos θ is positive at θ = 0 (stable, hanging) and negative at θ = π (unstable, inverted).
- For small oscillations about a stable equilibrium with kinetic energy ½mẋ², the natural frequency is ω = √(V″(x₀)/m). For the pendulum, using T = ½ml²θ̇², this gives ω = √(g/l).

Worked example
A spring of stiffness 200 N/m is compressed by 0.1 m and launches a 0.05 kg ball vertically. Stored energy = ½ × 200 × 0.1² = 1 J. Ignoring losses, the ball rises until mgh = 1 J, so h = 1/(0.05 × 9.81) = 2.04 m above the release point.

Exam tips: list which forces do work and which do not before writing an energy equation, and use energy to find speeds, then F = ma (or d'Alembert) to find the forces at that position.

notes.h: Linear momentum, impulse and variable-mass systems
notes.body:
Momentum methods are the natural tool for short, violent events (collisions, explosions) and for systems that gain or lose mass.

Linear momentum and impulse
- Linear momentum p = mv. Newton's second law is F = dp/dt.
- Integrating over time: the impulse ∫ F dt equals the change in momentum. Large forces acting for a short time are best handled as impulses.
- For a system of particles, internal forces cancel in pairs (third law). If the net external impulse in some direction is zero, total momentum in that direction is conserved.

Collisions between particles
- Momentum along the line of impact is conserved for the pair (if no external impulse acts).
- Newton's experimental law: (speed of separation) = e × (speed of approach), measured along the line of impact. The coefficient of restitution e lies between 0 (perfectly plastic, bodies move together) and 1 (perfectly elastic, no kinetic energy lost).
- Worked example: a 2 kg mass at 3 m/s hits a stationary 1 kg mass with e = 0.5. Momentum: 6 = 2v₁ + v₂. Restitution: v₂ − v₁ = 1.5. Solving: v₁ = 1.5 m/s, v₂ = 3.0 m/s. Kinetic energy falls from 9 J to 6.75 J; 2.25 J is lost to deformation, heat and sound.

Variable-mass systems
- Newton's second law in the form F = ma applies to a fixed collection of particles. When mass is gained or lost, apply the momentum principle to a fixed system over a short time δt, then let δt → 0.
- Rocket: if mass is ejected at rate ṁ with speed u relative to the rocket, the thrust is ṁu. With external force F_ext (gravity, drag), m dv/dt = ṁu + F_ext, where F_ext is measured in the direction of motion.
- With no external force, integrating gives the rocket equation Δv = u ln(m₀/m₁), where m₀ and m₁ are the initial and final masses. Example: u = 3000 m/s and m₀/m₁ = 5 give Δv = 3000 ln 5 ≈ 4.83 km/s.
- Conveyor belt: sand falling vertically onto a belt moving at speed v at rate ṁ must be given horizontal momentum ṁv per second, so the belt needs a force F = ṁv. The power supplied is ṁv², but the kinetic energy of the sand rises only at ½ṁv²; the other half is dissipated by friction as the sand slips and accelerates.

Exam tips: define the system and the time interval clearly before applying momentum, and never use energy conservation through an impact unless the question says it is elastic.

Angular momentum turns problems with a central force, such as gravity on a satellite, into a few lines of algebra.

Angular momentum of a particle
- About a fixed point O: h_O = r × mv, where r is measured from O.
- Differentiating: the moment of the forces about O equals dh_O/dt.
- If the force always passes through O (a central force), its moment about O is zero and h_O is conserved.
- In polar coordinates the transverse velocity is rθ̇, so h = mr²θ̇. Conservation means r²θ̇ is constant: the radius sweeps out equal areas in equal times (Kepler's second law).

Gravity and circular orbits
- Newton's law of gravitation: F = GMm/r², directed towards the centre of the Earth. For the Earth, GM ≈ 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³ s⁻², and GM = gR² where R is the Earth's radius.
- For a circular orbit, gravity supplies the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r, so v = √(GM/r).
- Period: T = 2πr/v = 2π√(r³/GM), so T² is proportional to r³ (Kepler's third law).
- Example: at 400 km altitude (r ≈ 6771 km), v ≈ 7.67 km/s and T ≈ 5545 s ≈ 92 minutes.
- Geostationary orbit: the period must equal one sidereal day (about 86,164 s), giving r = (GMT²/4π²)^(1/3) ≈ 42,160 km, about 35,800 km above the surface.

Energy and elliptical orbits
- Gravitational potential energy is V = −GMm/r (zero at infinity). Total energy per unit mass ½v² − GM/r is constant.
- For a bound elliptical orbit with semi-major axis a, the energy per unit mass is −GM/(2a). This gives the vis-viva equation v² = GM(2/r − 1/a).
- At perigee and apogee the velocity is perpendicular to the radius, so conservation of angular momentum gives r_p v_p = r_a v_a.
- Combining with energy: v_p = √(2GM r_a / (r_p(r_p + r_a))).
- Escape speed (energy zero) from radius r is √(2GM/r), which is √2 times the circular orbit speed there.

Orbit transfers
- A Hohmann transfer moves a satellite between two circular orbits using a half-ellipse that touches both. One tangential burn at the inner orbit puts it on the ellipse; a second at the outer orbit circularises it. Each Δv is the difference between the ellipse speed and the circular speed at that radius.

Exam tips: use angular momentum and energy together for any two points on an orbit, and keep r measured from the Earth's centre, not from the surface.

A rigid body is one in which the distance between any two points never changes. In plane motion its position is fixed by three numbers: two coordinates of a reference point and one angle.

Angular velocity
- Every line drawn on a rigid body in plane motion turns at the same rate. That rate is the angular velocity ω, which is a vector perpendicular to the plane (ω = θ̇ k). The angular acceleration is α = θ̈.

Relative velocity and acceleration of two points
- For two points A and B on the same rigid body: v_B = v_A + ω × r_AB.
- The relative velocity ω × r_AB has magnitude ω·AB and is perpendicular to AB. A rigid body can never have a component of relative velocity along the line joining two of its points.
- For accelerations in plane motion: a_B = a_A + α × r_AB − ω² r_AB. The last term points from B towards A (centripetal); the α term is perpendicular to AB.
- Velocity and acceleration diagrams, drawn to scale, are a graphical way of solving linkages using these relations.

Instantaneous centre of rotation
- At any instant in plane motion (other than pure translation) there is one point I, on the body or its extension, with zero velocity. Every other point moves as if the body were rotating about I: speed = ω × (distance from I), direction perpendicular to the line from I.
- To find I, draw lines perpendicular to the known velocity directions of two points; I is where they cross.
- I generally has non-zero acceleration, so it cannot be used for accelerations in the same simple way.
- Rolling without slipping: the contact point is the instantaneous centre. A wheel of radius R has v_G = ωR and a_G = αR. Example: R = 0.3 m at 6 m/s gives ω = 20 rad/s, and the top of the wheel moves at 12 m/s.
- Ladder example: a 5 m ladder with its foot B 3 m from a wall and top A 4 m up. If B slides out at 1.2 m/s, I is at (3, 4), so IB = 4 m, ω = 0.3 rad/s, and A moves down at 0.3 × 3 = 0.9 m/s.

Rotating reference frames
- For any vector A described in a frame rotating at ω: dA/dt = (dA/dt)_rel + ω × A.
- For a point P moving relative to a rotating body: v_P = v_O + ω × r + v_rel.
- a_P = a_O + α × r + ω × (ω × r) + 2ω × v_rel + a_rel. The term 2ω × v_rel is the Coriolis acceleration; it matches the 2ṙθ̇ term in polar coordinates.

Exam tips: sketch the body, mark known velocity directions, and look for the instantaneous centre first; it often reduces a velocity problem to one line of geometry.

notes.h: Centre of mass and moments of inertia
notes.body:
Rigid-body dynamics needs two properties of the body: where its mass is centred and how that mass is spread about an axis.

Centre of mass
- x̄ = Σmᵢxᵢ / Σmᵢ, or ∫x dm / m for a continuous body; similarly for ȳ.
- For a uniform lamina the centre of mass is at the centroid of the shape. Standard results: a triangle's centroid is one third of the height above its base; a semicircular lamina's is 4R/(3π) from the diameter.
- Composite bodies: split into simple parts, and treat holes as negative mass.
- The net external force on a body equals its total mass times the acceleration of its centre of mass.

Moment of inertia
- About a given axis: I = ∫r² dm, where r is the perpendicular distance from the axis. It measures resistance to angular acceleration, just as mass resists linear acceleration.
- Radius of gyration k: I = mk².
- Standard results for uniform bodies:
- Thin rod, length L, about a perpendicular axis through its centre: mL²/12; about a perpendicular axis through one end: mL²/3.
- Thin ring or hoop of radius R about its central axis: mR².
- Disc of radius R about its central axis (perpendicular to the disc): mR²/2.
- Rectangular plate a × b about a perpendicular axis through its centre: m(a² + b²)/12.

Parallel axis theorem
- I_O = I_G + md², where G is the centre of mass and d is the distance between the parallel axes through G and O.
- Example: rod about its end = mL²/12 + m(L/2)² = mL²/3.
- It only links to the axis through G; to move between two axes that are both away from G, go via G.

Perpendicular axis theorem
- For a lamina lying in the x–y plane: I_z = I_x + I_y, where all three axes pass through the same point.
- Example: a disc has I_z = mR²/2, and by symmetry I_x = I_y, so the moment of inertia about a diameter is mR²/4.
- It applies only to flat (planar) bodies.

Worked example
A disc of outer radius R with a concentric hole of radius r has I = ½ρπ(R⁴ − r⁴) = ½M(R² + r²), where M is the mass of the remaining annulus and ρ the mass per unit area.

Exam tips: always state the axis; build composite moments of inertia by parallel-axis shifts of standard results; and sanity-check that adding mass far from the axis increases I.

notes.h: Dynamics of rigid bodies in plane motion
notes.body:
This is where the course comes together: forces cause the centre of mass to accelerate, and moments cause the body to spin up.

Equations of planar motion
- Translation: ΣF = m a_G, where a_G is the acceleration of the centre of mass G.
- Rotation about G: ΣM_G = I_G α.
- Rotation about a fixed axis through O: ΣM_O = I_O α. This removes the unknown pivot reaction from the moment equation.
- Taking moments about any other point requires care. A safe method is d'Alembert's: add an inertia force −m a_G acting at G and an inertia couple −I_G α, then take moments about any convenient point as in statics.

Kinetic energy and angular momentum
- T = ½ m v_G² + ½ I_G ω². For pure rotation about a fixed axis O, T = ½ I_O ω².
- Angular momentum about G in plane motion is I_G ω.
- Energy methods apply just as for particles: if no work is lost (smooth contacts, rolling without slip), T + V is constant.

Worked example: rod released from horizontal
A uniform rod of mass m and length L is pivoted at end A and released from rest horizontally.
- Moments about A: mg(L/2) = (mL²/3)α, so α = 3g/(2L).
- G accelerates downwards at α(L/2) = 3g/4. Vertically: mg − R = m(3g/4), so the pivot reaction R = mg/4.
- When vertical, energy gives mgL/2 = ½(mL²/3)ω², so ω² = 3g/L. Then α = 0 and G has centripetal acceleration ω²L/2 = 3g/2 upwards, so R − mg = 3mg/2 and R = 5mg/2.

Worked example: disc rolling down a slope
A uniform disc rolls without slipping down a slope at angle θ.
- Along the slope: mg sin θ − F = ma. Moments about G: FR = (mR²/2)α with a = αR.
- So F = ma/2 and a = (2/3) g sin θ, F = (1/3) mg sin θ.
- Rolling needs F ≤ μN = μmg cos θ, so μ ≥ (1/3) tan θ.
- A hoop gives a = (1/2) g sin θ; a frictionless sliding block gives g sin θ. Bodies with more mass far from the axis roll down more slowly.

Worked example: hanging mass on a flywheel
A rope wound on a drum of radius r (I = 0.5 kg m², r = 0.2 m) carries a 5 kg mass. For the mass mg − T = ma; for the drum Tr = Iα = Ia/r. So a = mg/(m + I/r²) = 49.05/17.5 = 2.80 m/s² and T = 35.0 N.

Exam tips: draw the free-body diagram with all reactions, write one equation per degree of freedom plus the kinematic link (such as a = αR), and say whether friction is static (unknown, ≤ μN) or sliding (= μN).

notes.h: Impulse, momentum and impact of rigid bodies
notes.body:
Impact problems combine momentum ideas from particles with rigid-body rotation. They are a favourite final part of Part IA questions.

Impulse and momentum for a rigid body
- Linear: the net external impulse equals m Δv_G.
- Angular, about G: the net moment of impulse about G equals I_G Δω.
- About a fixed pivot O: the moment of impulse about O equals I_O Δω.
- For a general point, the angular momentum of a body in plane motion about a fixed point O is m(r_G × v_G) + I_G ω.

Assumptions during an impact
- The impact lasts a very short time, so positions do not change during it.
- Impulsive forces (contact forces at the impact, reactions at pivots that resist the impact) are very large; ordinary finite forces such as gravity or springs give negligible impulse and are ignored.
- Choose the point about which to take angular momentum so that unknown impulses pass through it; angular momentum about that point is then conserved.
- Kinetic energy is not conserved in general. Use the coefficient of restitution e on the normal components of velocity of the two contact points: separation speed = e × approach speed.

Worked example: rod hitting a peg
A uniform rod (mass m, length L) moves sideways without rotating at speed v and its end catches on a fixed peg, about which it then pivots. The peg impulse passes through the peg, so angular momentum about the peg is conserved: mv(L/2) = (mL²/3)ω, giving ω = 3v/(2L). Kinetic energy after = ½(mL²/3)ω² = (3/8)mv², so three quarters of the original ½mv² is retained.

Worked example: centre of percussion
A rod pivoted at one end is struck at distance b from the pivot by an impulse J. For no impulse at the pivot, linear momentum needs J = mω(L/2) and angular momentum about the pivot needs Jb = (mL²/3)ω. Hence b = 2L/3. Striking here (the "sweet spot") sends no shock into the pivot.

Worked example: engaging a clutch
Disc A (I = 0.2 kg m², spinning at 100 rad/s) is clutched to disc B (I = 0.3 kg m², at rest) on the same axis. The clutch torques are internal, so angular momentum is conserved: 0.2 × 100 = 0.5ω, giving ω = 40 rad/s. Kinetic energy falls from 1000 J to 400 J; 600 J is dissipated in the clutch.

Exam tips: split the problem into before, during and after the impact; use energy only before and after, and use momentum (with restitution if needed) across the impact itself.

cards.b: The net external force equals the rate of change of linear momentum, F = d(mv)/dt. For constant mass this reduces to F = ma.
Forces between two bodies come in equal and opposite pairs acting along the same line, one on each body. They never act on the same body, so they never cancel in one free-body diagram.
1 N = 1 kg m s⁻²: the force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s².
With no slip the friction force F can take any value up to μN. During slip F = μN and acts to oppose the relative sliding motion.
A frame in which Newton's laws hold without extra terms. Any frame moving at constant velocity relative to an inertial frame is also inertial; accelerating or rotating frames are not.
A sketch of one body (or chosen system) isolated from its surroundings, showing every external force acting on it with its direction and point of action. Internal forces are left out.

cards.f: Acceleration of a block sliding down a rough incline (angle θ, friction coefficient μ)
cards.b: a = g(sin θ − μ cos θ), from resolving along and normal to the slope with sliding friction μN acting up the slope.
v = ṙ e_r + rθ̇ e_θ: radial component ṙ, transverse component rθ̇.
a = (r̈ − rθ̇²) e_r + (rθ̈ + 2ṙθ̇) e_θ.

cards.f: Derivatives of the polar unit vectors
cards.b: de_r/dt = θ̇ e_θ and de_θ/dt = −θ̇ e_r. They arise because the unit vectors rotate with the particle.
a = v̇ e_t + (v²/ρ) e_n: tangential component v̇ along the path, normal component v²/ρ towards the centre of curvature.
The Coriolis term in the transverse acceleration in polar coordinates. It appears when the radius and the angle change at the same time.

cards.f: Central difference for velocity from sampled positions
cards.b: v_n ≈ (x_{n+1} − x_{n−1}) / (2Δt), where Δt is the sampling interval.
v_B = v_A + v_B/A, found by differentiating r_B = r_A + r_B/A; valid when the relative quantities are measured in a non-rotating frame.
The fictitious inertia force −ma added to the real forces so that F + (−ma) = 0, letting a dynamics problem be solved like statics.

cards.f: Forward Euler update for x and v
cards.b: x_{n+1} = x_n + v_n Δt and v_{n+1} = v_n + a_n Δt, using values at the start of each step.

cards.f: Turning a second-order ODE into first-order form
cards.b: Introduce v = ẋ, so ẍ = f(x, ẋ, t) becomes the pair ẋ = v and v̇ = f(x, v, t), which numerical solvers can step forward.

cards.f: How to check a numerical solution
cards.b: Halve the time step and confirm the answer barely changes, and test the code on a case with a known exact solution.

cards.f: Bead released from rest (relative to the rod) at r₀ on a smooth rod rotating at constant ω
cards.b: r = r₀ cosh ωt, and the transverse force from the rod is N = 2mω²r₀ sinh ωt.

cards.f: Weakness of forward Euler for an undamped oscillator
cards.b: Its error is proportional to Δt and it steadily adds energy, so the computed amplitude grows even though the true motion has constant amplitude.
W = ∫ F · dr: only the component of force along the displacement does work.
The total work done on a particle by all forces equals its change in kinetic energy ½mv².
For a conservative force, F = −dV/dx: the force points down the slope of the potential energy.
dV/dq = 0 and d²V/dq² > 0, i.e. a minimum of potential energy. A maximum (d²V/dq² < 0) is unstable.

cards.f: Gravitational potential energy far from the Earth
cards.b: V = −GMm/r, taking zero at infinity.

cards.f: Frequency of small oscillations from potential energy
cards.b: For kinetic energy ½mẋ², ω = √(V″(x₀)/m), where x₀ is the stable equilibrium.
The rate of doing work: P = F · v (watts).
The impulse ∫F dt of the net external force equals the change in linear momentum m Δv.
Speed of separation = e × speed of approach along the line of impact; e = 1 is perfectly elastic, e = 0 perfectly plastic.
When the net external impulse on the chosen system is zero in that direction; internal forces cancel by Newton's third law.
ṁu, where ṁ is the rate of mass ejection and u the exhaust speed relative to the rocket.
Δv = u ln(m₀/m₁), with m₀ and m₁ the initial and final masses.

cards.f: Force to keep a conveyor at speed v while material lands on it at rate ṁ
cards.b: F = ṁv. The power ṁv² is twice the rate of gain of kinetic energy; half is dissipated by friction as the material is accelerated.

cards.f: Angular momentum of a particle about O
cards.b: h_O = r × mv, with r measured from O. Its rate of change equals the moment of the forces about O.

cards.f: Why r²θ̇ is constant in a central-force orbit
cards.b: The force passes through the centre, so its moment is zero and angular momentum mr²θ̇ is conserved (Kepler's second law).
v = √(GM/r), from GMm/r² = mv²/r.
T = 2π√(r³/GM), so T² ∝ r³ (Kepler's third law).
v² = GM(2/r − 1/a), where a is the semi-major axis of the elliptical orbit.
√(2GM/r), which is √2 times the circular orbit speed at that radius.
About 42,160 km from the Earth's centre (about 35,800 km altitude), giving a period of one sidereal day.

cards.f: Velocity of B relative to A on a rigid body
cards.b: v_B = v_A + ω × r_AB: magnitude ω·AB, perpendicular to AB.

cards.f: Acceleration of B relative to A (plane motion)
cards.b: a_B = a_A + α × r_AB − ω² r_AB: a tangential part α·AB and a centripetal part ω²·AB directed from B towards A.
The point with zero velocity at that instant; found where lines perpendicular to the velocities of two points cross.
The contact point is the instantaneous centre, so v_G = ωR and a_G = αR for a wheel of radius R.

cards.f: Derivative of a vector in a rotating frame
cards.b: dA/dt = (dA/dt)_rel + ω × A.
2ω × v_rel, present when a point moves relative to a rotating frame.

cards.f: Speed of the top of a wheel rolling at speed v
cards.b: 2v, because it is 2R from the contact point, which is the instantaneous centre.
I = ∫r² dm about a stated axis, r being the perpendicular distance from the axis.
The distance k such that I = mk².
I_O = I_G + md², where the axis through O is parallel to one through the centre of mass G and d apart.
For a lamina in the x–y plane, I_z = I_x + I_y about axes through the same point. Valid only for flat bodies.

cards.f: Uniform rod about its centre and about its end
cards.b: mL²/12 about the centre; mL²/3 about one end (both axes perpendicular to the rod).

cards.f: Uniform disc about its axis and about a diameter
cards.b: mR²/2 about the central axis; mR²/4 about a diameter.
On the axis of symmetry, 4R/(3π) from the straight edge.
ΣF = m a_G and ΣM_G = I_G α. For a fixed axis O, ΣM_O = I_O α.

cards.f: Kinetic energy of a rigid body in plane motion
cards.b: T = ½ m v_G² + ½ I_G ω².

cards.f: Angular acceleration of a rod released from rest horizontally, pivoted at one end
cards.b: α = 3g/(2L), with pivot reaction mg/4 at that instant.

cards.f: Acceleration of a uniform disc rolling down a slope
cards.b: (2/3) g sin θ, with friction force (1/3) mg sin θ.

cards.f: Condition for a disc to roll without slipping down a slope of angle θ
cards.b: μ ≥ (1/3) tan θ, because the needed friction (1/3)mg sin θ must not exceed μmg cos θ.
Add an inertia force −m a_G at G and an inertia couple −I_G α, then take moments about any convenient point as in statics.

cards.f: Angular impulse–momentum for a rigid body
cards.b: The moment of impulse about G equals I_G Δω; about a fixed pivot O it equals I_O Δω.
Finite forces such as gravity and springs: their impulse over the very short impact time is negligible compared with impulsive contact forces.

cards.f: Choosing the point for angular momentum in an impact
cards.b: Take moments about the point through which the unknown impulses act, so their moment is zero and angular momentum about it is conserved.

cards.f: Centre of percussion of a rod pivoted at one end
cards.b: 2L/3 from the pivot: an impulse there produces no impulsive reaction at the pivot.

cards.f: Angular velocity of a translating rod (speed v) that catches a peg at its end
cards.b: ω = 3v/(2L), from mv(L/2) = (mL²/3)ω; it keeps 3/4 of its kinetic energy.

cards.f: Is kinetic energy conserved in an impact?
cards.b: Not in general. It is conserved only for a perfectly elastic impact (e = 1); otherwise use momentum and restitution.

questions.q: A 2 kg block slides down a rough plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal, with coefficient of friction 0.2. Taking g = 9.81 m/s², what is its acceleration down the slope?
questions.why: a = g(sin 30° − μ cos 30°) = 9.81(0.5 − 0.173) = 3.21 m/s². 4.91 m/s² ignores friction; 6.60 m/s² adds friction as if it helped the motion; 1.70 m/s² is just the friction term μg cos 30°.

questions.q: Which of these frames of reference is inertial (to the usual engineering approximation)?
options: A frame fixed to a turntable rotating at constant speed
A frame fixed in a lift accelerating upwards
A frame moving at constant velocity relative to the ground
A frame fixed in a car that is braking
questions.why: A frame moving at constant velocity relative to an inertial frame (the ground, approximately) is itself inertial. The rotating turntable, accelerating lift and braking car all accelerate, so Newton's laws need extra (fictitious) terms in them.

questions.q: A 70 kg person stands on bathroom scales in a lift that is accelerating upwards at 2 m/s². Using g = 9.81 m/s², find the reading on the scales in newtons, showing your free-body diagram reasoning.
markScheme: Free-body diagram of the person: weight mg down, normal reaction N from the scales up
Newton's second law upwards: N − mg = ma
N = 827 N (about 827 N), which is what the scales read; larger than the weight of 687 N
questions.modelAnswer: The forces on the person are the weight mg = 70 × 9.81 = 686.7 N acting downwards and the normal reaction N from the scales acting upwards. The person accelerates upwards with the lift at 2 m/s², so Newton's second law upwards gives N − mg = ma. Hence N = m(g + a) = 70 × (9.81 + 2) = 826.7 N. By Newton's third law the person pushes down on the scales with the same force, so the scales read about 827 N, more than the person's weight.

questions.q: In polar coordinates, what is the radial component of a particle's acceleration?
questions.why: Differentiating v = ṙ e_r + rθ̇ e_θ and using de_θ/dt = −θ̇ e_r gives a radial component r̈ − rθ̇². The plus sign is wrong because the centripetal term points inwards; rθ̈ + 2ṙθ̇ is the transverse component; r̈ alone ignores the rotation of the unit vectors.

questions.q: A car travels at 20 m/s round a bend of radius 50 m and is braking at 3 m/s². What is the magnitude of its acceleration?
questions.why: The normal component is v²/ρ = 400/50 = 8 m/s² and the tangential component is 3 m/s². They are perpendicular, so |a| = √(64 + 9) = 8.54 m/s². 11.0 adds them as scalars; 8.00 ignores braking; 3.00 ignores cornering.

questions.q: A slider moves outwards along a straight radial slot in a disc that rotates at a constant 2 rad/s. At one instant the slider is 0.5 m from the centre, moving outwards along the slot at 0.3 m/s, with no acceleration relative to the slot. Find the radial and transverse components of its acceleration and the magnitude of the total acceleration.
markScheme: Uses polar acceleration a_r = r̈ − rθ̇², a_θ = rθ̈ + 2ṙθ̇
Substitutes r̈ = 0, θ̈ = 0, θ̇ = 2 rad/s, r = 0.5 m, ṙ = 0.3 m/s
a_r = −2.0 m/s² (i.e. 2.0 m/s² towards the centre)
a_θ = 1.2 m/s² (Coriolis term)
questions.modelAnswer: Use polar coordinates with the origin at the disc centre. Here r = 0.5 m, ṙ = 0.3 m/s, r̈ = 0, θ̇ = 2 rad/s and θ̈ = 0. Radial: a_r = r̈ − rθ̇² = 0 − 0.5 × 4 = −2.0 m/s², i.e. 2.0 m/s² towards the centre. Transverse: a_θ = rθ̈ + 2ṙθ̇ = 0 + 2 × 0.3 × 2 = 1.2 m/s² in the direction of rotation; this is the Coriolis term. Magnitude: √(2.0² + 1.2²) = √5.44 ≈ 2.33 m/s².

questions.q: The equation ẍ = −x is integrated by forward Euler with x₀ = 0, v₀ = 1 and Δt = 0.1. What are x and v after two steps?
questions.why: Step 1: x₁ = 0 + 1 × 0.1 = 0.1; v₁ = 1 + (−0)(0.1) = 1. Step 2: x₂ = 0.1 + 1 × 0.1 = 0.2; v₂ = 1 + (−0.1)(0.1) = 0.99. v = 1.00 forgets to update v at step 2; 0.199 is close to the exact sin(0.2) rather than the Euler value; 0.19, 0.98 does not follow from the update rule.

questions.q: What does d'Alembert's principle allow you to do?
options: Treat −ma as an extra force so that the forces sum to zero, as in statics
Replace Newton's second law with energy conservation
Assume the acceleration of a body is zero at equilibrium
questions.why: d'Alembert writes F − ma = 0 and treats −ma as an inertia force, so equilibrium methods (including taking moments about any point) can be used. It says nothing about friction, it is not an energy method, and it does not require zero acceleration.

questions.q: A smooth straight rod rotates in a horizontal plane at constant angular velocity ω about a vertical axis through one end O. A bead of mass m is released at distance r₀ from O with no velocity along the rod. Show that r = r₀ cosh ωt and find the horizontal force the rod exerts on the bead as a function of time.
markScheme: Radial equation: no radial force on a smooth rod, so m(r̈ − rω²) = 0
General solution r = A cosh ωt + B sinh ωt (or exponentials)
Initial conditions r(0) = r₀, ṙ(0) = 0 give r = r₀ cosh ωt
Transverse equation N = m(rθ̈ + 2ṙθ̇) with θ̈ = 0
N = 2mω²r₀ sinh ωt, perpendicular to the rod in the direction of rotation
questions.modelAnswer: Use polar coordinates centred on O, with θ̇ = ω constant. The rod is smooth, so it can exert no force along itself; gravity is vertical and balanced by a vertical reaction. Radially: m(r̈ − rω²) = 0, so r̈ = ω²r. The general solution is r = A cosh ωt + B sinh ωt. At t = 0, r = r₀ gives A = r₀, and ṙ = 0 gives B = 0, so r = r₀ cosh ωt. Transversely the only horizontal force is the rod's normal force N: N = m(rθ̈ + 2ṙθ̇) = 2mωṙ. Since ṙ = r₀ω sinh ωt, N = 2mω²r₀ sinh ωt, acting perpendicular to the rod in the direction of rotation. The force grows rapidly with time because the bead's radial speed grows.

questions.q: A system has potential energy V(x) = x³ − 3x. Which statement about its equilibrium positions is correct?
options: x = 1 is stable and x = −1 is unstable
x = 1 is unstable and x = −1 is stable
Both x = 1 and x = −1 are stable
The only equilibrium is at x = 0
questions.why: dV/dx = 3x² − 3 = 0 at x = ±1. d²V/dx² = 6x is +6 at x = 1 (a minimum, stable) and −6 at x = −1 (a maximum, unstable). x = 0 is not an equilibrium because dV/dx = −3 there.

questions.q: A spring of stiffness 200 N/m is compressed by 0.1 m and launches a 0.05 kg ball straight up. Ignoring losses and taking g = 9.81 m/s², how high does the ball rise above the release point?
questions.why: Stored energy ½kx² = ½ × 200 × 0.01 = 1 J = mgh, so h = 1/(0.05 × 9.81) = 2.04 m. 4.08 m omits the ½ in the spring energy; 1.02 m includes an extra factor of ½ (half the correct height); 20.0 m forgets g.

questions.q: A simple pendulum consists of a particle of mass m on a light rod of length l, free to swing in a vertical plane about a fixed pivot. Using potential energy, find its equilibrium positions, state which is stable, and use energy to find the natural frequency of small oscillations about the stable position.
markScheme: V = −mgl cos θ (θ measured from the downward vertical)
dV/dθ = mgl sin θ = 0 gives θ = 0 and θ = π
d²V/dθ² = mgl cos θ: positive at θ = 0 (stable), negative at θ = π (unstable)
T + V constant with T = ½ml²θ̇²; differentiate (or use small-angle form) to get ml²θ̈ + mglθ = 0
questions.modelAnswer: Measure θ from the downward vertical. The height of the particle above the pivot is −l cos θ, so V = −mgl cos θ. Equilibria: dV/dθ = mgl sin θ = 0, so θ = 0 (hanging) or θ = π (inverted). d²V/dθ² = mgl cos θ, which is +mgl at θ = 0, a minimum, so this is stable; it is −mgl at θ = π, a maximum, so the inverted position is unstable. Energy: ½ml²θ̇² − mgl cos θ = constant. Differentiating with respect to time: ml²θ̇θ̈ + mgl sin θ θ̇ = 0, so ml²θ̈ + mgl sin θ = 0. For small θ, sin θ ≈ θ, giving θ̈ + (g/l)θ = 0, which is simple harmonic motion with ω = √(g/l).

questions.q: A 2 kg mass moving at 3 m/s collides head-on with a stationary 1 kg mass. The coefficient of restitution is 0.5. What are the velocities of the 2 kg and 1 kg masses after impact?
questions.why: Momentum: 6 = 2v₁ + v₂. Restitution: v₂ − v₁ = 0.5 × 3 = 1.5. Solving gives v₁ = 1.5 m/s and v₂ = 3.0 m/s. 2.0 and 2.0 m/s is the perfectly plastic case (e = 0); 1.0 and 4.0 m/s is the elastic case (e = 1); 0 and 6.0 m/s conserves momentum but breaks the restitution law.

questions.q: A rocket with exhaust speed 3000 m/s (relative to the rocket) burns fuel until its mass falls to one fifth of its initial value. Ignoring gravity and drag, what is its gain in speed?
questions.why: Δv = u ln(m₀/m₁) = 3000 ln 5 = 4828 m/s ≈ 4.83 km/s. 2.10 km/s uses log base 10; 12.0 km/s uses (5 − 1) × u; 15.0 km/s multiplies u by the mass ratio.

questions.q: Sand falls vertically onto a horizontal conveyor belt at 20 kg/s. The belt moves at a constant 2 m/s. Find the extra horizontal force needed to keep the belt moving, the power this requires, and the rate at which the sand gains kinetic energy. Explain the difference.
markScheme: Each second 20 kg of sand gains horizontal momentum 20 × 2 = 40 kg m/s
So the horizontal force needed is F = ṁv = 40 N
Power = Fv = 80 W
Rate of gain of kinetic energy = ½ṁv² = 40 W
The other 40 W is dissipated as heat by friction while the sand slips and is accelerated up to belt speed
questions.modelAnswer: Consider the sand that lands in a short time δt: mass ṁδt arrives with no horizontal velocity and leaves with the belt speed v. Its horizontal momentum rises by ṁδt·v, so the belt must supply a horizontal force F = ṁv = 20 × 2 = 40 N. The motor's extra power is Fv = 40 × 2 = 80 W. The sand's kinetic energy increases at ½ṁv² = ½ × 20 × 4 = 40 W. The remaining 40 W, exactly half, is dissipated by friction as each grain slides on the belt before it reaches belt speed. Energy is not conserved in this process, which is why momentum, not energy, must be used to find the force.

questions.q: Roughly what is the orbital period of a satellite in a circular orbit 400 km above the Earth's surface?
questions.why: With r = 6771 km and GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³ s⁻², T = 2π√(r³/GM) ≈ 5545 s ≈ 92 min. 24 hours is geostationary; about 84 minutes is the period of a hypothetical orbit at the Earth's surface; 9 minutes is physically impossible, since even an orbit skimming the surface takes about 84 minutes.

questions.q: A satellite moves under the Earth's gravity alone. Which quantity stays constant (r measured from the Earth's centre)?
questions.why: Gravity is a central force, so angular momentum mr²θ̇ is conserved, and hence r²θ̇. Speed is only constant for a circular orbit; rθ̇ (transverse speed) and rθ̇² change as r changes on an ellipse.

questions.q: A satellite moves in an elliptical orbit about the Earth with perigee radius 7000 km and apogee radius 14,000 km (both measured from the Earth's centre). Taking GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³ s⁻², find its speeds at perigee and apogee.
markScheme: Angular momentum conserved; velocity perpendicular to radius at both apses, so r_p v_p = r_a v_a, giving v_a = v_p/2
Energy conserved: ½v_p² − GM/r_p = ½v_a² − GM/r_a
Solves to v_p = √(2GM r_a / (r_p(r_p + r_a)))
v_p ≈ 8.71 km/s
v_a ≈ 4.36 km/s
questions.modelAnswer: At perigee and apogee the velocity is perpendicular to the radius, so conservation of angular momentum gives r_p v_p = r_a v_a. Here r_a = 2r_p, so v_a = v_p/2. Energy conservation: ½v_p² − GM/r_p = ½v_a² − GM/r_a. Substituting v_a = v_p r_p/r_a and rearranging gives v_p² = 2GM r_a / (r_p(r_p + r_a)) = 2 × 3.986 × 10¹⁴ × 14 × 10⁶ / (7 × 10⁶ × 21 × 10⁶) = 7.592 × 10⁷ m²/s². So v_p ≈ 8713 m/s ≈ 8.71 km/s, and v_a = v_p/2 ≈ 4.36 km/s. Check: the energy per unit mass at each point is about −1.898 × 10⁷ J/kg, equal to −GM/(r_p + r_a) = −GM/(2a) as expected.

questions.q: A wheel of radius 0.3 m rolls without slipping along level ground with its centre moving at 6 m/s. How fast is the highest point of the wheel moving?
questions.why: The contact point is the instantaneous centre, so ω = 6/0.3 = 20 rad/s and the top, 0.6 m from the contact point, moves at 20 × 0.6 = 12 m/s. 6 m/s is the centre's speed; 0 m/s is the contact point; 8.5 m/s (6√2) is the speed of a point level with the centre on the rim.

questions.q: A point P moves with velocity v_rel relative to a body rotating at angular velocity ω. Which term in the acceleration of P is the Coriolis acceleration?
questions.why: The Coriolis term is 2ω × v_rel. ω × (ω × r) is the centripetal term; α × r is the tangential term from angular acceleration; a_rel is the acceleration measured in the rotating frame.

questions.q: A ladder AB of length 5 m has its top A against a smooth vertical wall and its foot B on smooth level ground. At an instant when B is 3 m from the wall and moving away from it at 1.2 m/s, find the angular velocity of the ladder and the velocity of A.
markScheme: A is 4 m above the ground (3-4-5 triangle)
v_B is horizontal and v_A is vertical; the perpendiculars meet at the instantaneous centre I, 3 m from the wall and 4 m up
v_A = ω × IA = 0.3 × 3 = 0.9 m/s, downwards
Check by constraint x² + y² = 25: xẋ + yẏ = 0 gives ẏ = −0.9 m/s
questions.modelAnswer: Put the origin at the base of the wall. B is at (3, 0) and A is at (0, 4), since √(5² − 3²) = 4 m. B moves horizontally, so I lies on the vertical line through B; A moves vertically, so I lies on the horizontal line through A. Hence I is at (3, 4). The distance IB = 4 m, so ω = 1.2/4 = 0.3 rad/s. The distance IA = 3 m, so A moves at 0.3 × 3 = 0.9 m/s, downwards. Check: x² + y² = 25 gives xẋ + yẏ = 0, so 3 × 1.2 + 4ẏ = 0 and ẏ = −0.9 m/s.

questions.q: What is the moment of inertia of a uniform thin rod of mass m and length L about an axis perpendicular to it through one end?
questions.why: By the parallel axis theorem, I = mL²/12 + m(L/2)² = mL²/3. mL²/12 is about the centre; mL²/4 is just the md² term; mL² would put all the mass at the far end.

questions.q: A uniform disc has mass m and radius R. What is its moment of inertia about a diameter?
questions.why: By the perpendicular axis theorem I_z = I_x + I_y, and by symmetry I_x = I_y, so I_diameter = (mR²/2)/2 = mR²/4. mR²/2 is about the central axis; mR² is a ring; 3mR²/2 is the disc about a parallel axis through its rim.

questions.q: A pendulum is made from a uniform rod (mass 1 kg, length 0.6 m), pivoted at one end, with a uniform disc (mass 2 kg, radius 0.1 m) fixed with its centre at the other end of the rod. The disc lies in the plane of swing. Find the distance of the centre of mass from the pivot and the moment of inertia about the pivot.
markScheme: Centre of mass: (1 × 0.3 + 2 × 0.6)/3 = 0.5 m from the pivot
Rod about its end: mL²/3 = 0.12 kg m²
Disc about its own centre (axis perpendicular to disc): MR²/2 = 0.01 kg m²
Parallel axis shift for the disc: Md² = 2 × 0.6² = 0.72 kg m²
Total I = 0.85 kg m²
questions.modelAnswer: Centre of mass: the rod's mass acts at 0.3 m and the disc's at 0.6 m from the pivot, so x̄ = (1 × 0.3 + 2 × 0.6)/(1 + 2) = 1.5/3 = 0.5 m. Moment of inertia about the pivot (axis perpendicular to the plane of swing): rod about its end = (1)(0.6²)/3 = 0.12 kg m². Disc about its own centre = (2)(0.1²)/2 = 0.01 kg m²; shifting to the pivot by the parallel axis theorem adds 2 × 0.6² = 0.72 kg m², so the disc contributes 0.73 kg m². Total I = 0.12 + 0.73 = 0.85 kg m².

questions.q: A uniform rod of length L, pivoted freely at one end, is released from rest in a horizontal position. What is its initial angular acceleration?
questions.why: Moments about the pivot: mg(L/2) = (mL²/3)α, so α = 3g/(2L). g/L treats the rod as a point mass at L; 3g/L forgets the factor ½ in the lever arm; 2g/(3L) inverts the ratio.

questions.q: A uniform solid disc rolls without slipping down a slope inclined at θ. What is the acceleration of its centre?
questions.why: mg sin θ − F = ma and FR = (mR²/2)(a/R) give a = (2/3) g sin θ. g sin θ is a frictionless slide; (1/2) g sin θ is a thin hoop (I = mR²); (5/7) g sin θ is a solid sphere (I = 2mR²/5).

questions.q: A light rope is wound round a drum of radius 0.2 m whose moment of inertia about its fixed horizontal axle is 0.5 kg m². A 5 kg mass hangs from the free end of the rope and is released from rest. Ignoring bearing friction and taking g = 9.81 m/s², find the acceleration of the mass and the rope tension.
markScheme: Mass: mg − T = ma
Drum: Tr = Iα
Kinematic link (rope does not slip): a = αr
questions.modelAnswer: For the hanging mass, downwards: mg − T = ma. For the drum, moments about the axle: Tr = Iα. The rope does not slip, so a = αr, giving T = Ia/r². Substituting: mg = a(m + I/r²), so a = 5 × 9.81 / (5 + 0.5/0.04) = 49.05/17.5 = 2.80 m/s². Then T = 12.5 × 2.80 = 35.0 N. Check: mg − T = 49.05 − 35.0 = 14.0 N = 5 × 2.80. The tension is less than the weight (49.05 N), as it must be if the mass accelerates downwards.

questions.q: A uniform rod of length L moves sideways (without rotating) at speed v perpendicular to its length. One end catches on a fixed peg and the rod then pivots about it. What is its angular velocity just after the impact?
questions.why: The peg impulse passes through the peg, so angular momentum about it is conserved: mv(L/2) = (mL²/3)ω, giving ω = 3v/(2L). v/(2L) and 3v/L come from wrong lever arms or inertia; v/L assumes the far end keeps speed v.

questions.q: A uniform rod of length L hangs from a pivot at its upper end. At what distance below the pivot should a horizontal blow be struck so that there is no impulsive reaction at the pivot?
questions.why: No pivot impulse needs J = mω(L/2) and J b = (mL²/3)ω, so b = 2L/3, the centre of percussion. At L/2 (the centre of mass) the rod would need a pivot impulse to stop the top moving; L and L/3 do not satisfy both equations.

questions.q: Disc A (moment of inertia 0.2 kg m²) spins at 100 rad/s. It is engaged through a friction clutch with disc B (moment of inertia 0.3 kg m²), initially at rest on the same axis, until they turn together. Find the final angular velocity and the energy dissipated in the clutch.
markScheme: Clutch torques are internal to the two-disc system, so angular momentum is conserved
Initial kinetic energy ½ × 0.2 × 100² = 1000 J
Final kinetic energy ½ × 0.5 × 40² = 400 J
Energy dissipated = 600 J (as heat in the clutch)
questions.modelAnswer: The friction torques in the clutch act equally and oppositely on the two discs, so they are internal to the system and total angular momentum about the axis is conserved: 0.2 × 100 = (0.2 + 0.3)ω, so ω = 20/0.5 = 40 rad/s. Kinetic energy before = ½ × 0.2 × 100² = 1000 J. After = ½ × 0.5 × 40² = 400 J. So 600 J is dissipated as heat in the clutch while the plates slip. As in a perfectly plastic collision, energy is lost even though momentum is conserved.

questions.q:
A uniform rod AB of mass m and length L is freely pivoted at A about a fixed horizontal axis. It is released from rest with AB horizontal.
(a) Find the angular acceleration of the rod and the vertical reaction at the pivot at the instant of release. [5]
(b) Find the angular velocity ω₀ of the rod and the reaction at the pivot when the rod reaches the vertical. [6]
(c) At the vertical, end B strikes a small block of mass m resting on a smooth horizontal floor. The impact is perfectly elastic. Find the velocity of the block and the angular velocity of the rod immediately after the impact, and verify that kinetic energy is conserved. [7]
(d) Find the horizontal impulse exerted by the pivot during the impact. [2]
markScheme: (a) Moments about A: mg(L/2) = (mL²/3)α, so α = 3g/(2L)
(a) a_G = αL/2 = 3g/4 downwards; mg − R = 3mg/4, so R = mg/4 upwards
(b) Energy: mgL/2 = ½(mL²/3)ω₀², so ω₀ = √(3g/L)
(b) At vertical α = 0 (no moment about A); centripetal a_G = ω₀²L/2 = 3g/2 upwards; R − mg = 3mg/2 so R = 5mg/2 (no horizontal reaction)
(c) Angular momentum about A conserved (pivot impulse passes through A): (mL²/3)ω₀ = (mL²/3)ω₁ + m v L
(c) Restitution e = 1 at B: v − ω₁L = ω₀L
(c) Solving: v = ω₀L/2 = ½√(3gL), ω₁ = −ω₀/2 (rod rebounds); kinetic energy before and after both equal mL²ω₀²/6 = mgL/2
(d) Linear momentum of system before mω₀L/2, after mω₁L/2 + mv = mω₀L/4; pivot impulse = −mω₀L/4, i.e. mω₀L/4 = (m/4)√(3gL) opposite to the block's motion
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) At release, the only forces are the weight mg at G (L/2 from A) and the pivot reaction at A. Moments about A: mg(L/2) = I_A α with I_A = mL²/3, so α = 3g/(2L). The rod is at rest, so G has no centripetal acceleration and its acceleration is αL/2 = 3g/4, vertically downwards. Vertically: mg − R = m(3g/4), so R = mg/4 upwards. There is no horizontal reaction because G has no horizontal acceleration.

(b) Energy from release to vertical: G falls L/2, so mgL/2 = ½(mL²/3)ω₀², giving ω₀² = 3g/L and ω₀ = √(3g/L). With the rod vertical, the weight passes through A, so α = 0. G then has only centripetal acceleration ω₀²(L/2) = 3g/2 towards A (upwards). Vertically: R − mg = m(3g/2), so R = 5mg/2 upwards, with no horizontal component.

(c) During the impact the only impulses are at B (horizontal) and at the pivot A. Taking angular momentum about A removes the pivot impulse. Let ω₁ be the rod's angular velocity after impact (same sense as ω₀ positive) and v the block's velocity. Angular momentum about A: (mL²/3)ω₀ = (mL²/3)ω₁ + mvL. Dividing by mL²/3 and writing V = v/L: ω₀ = ω₁ + 3V. Restitution with e = 1 at B, whose speed is ω₀L before and ω₁L after: v − ω₁L = ω₀L, so V = ω₀ + ω₁. Substituting: ω₀ = ω₁ + 3ω₀ + 3ω₁, so ω₁ = −ω₀/2 and V = ω₀/2. Hence the block moves off at v = ω₀L/2 = ½√(3gL) and the rod swings back with angular velocity ω₀/2.
Energy check: before, ½(mL²/3)ω₀² = mL²ω₀²/6. After, ½(mL²/3)(ω₀²/4) + ½m(ω₀L/2)² = mL²ω₀²/24 + mL²ω₀²/8 = mL²ω₀²/6. These are equal (both mgL/2), as expected for e = 1.

(d) Horizontal linear momentum of rod plus block: before, m(ω₀L/2) (velocity of G times m); after, m(ω₁L/2) + mv = −mω₀L/4 + mω₀L/2 = mω₀L/4. The change, −mω₀L/4, must be supplied by the pivot. So the pivot exerts a horizontal impulse of magnitude mω₀L/4 = (m/4)√(3gL), directed opposite to the block's motion. The point of impact (B, at distance L) is not the centre of percussion (2L/3), which is why there is a pivot impulse.

questions.q:
Take GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³ s⁻² for the Earth and the Earth's radius as 6371 km.
(a) Show that a satellite in a circular orbit of radius r has speed √(GM/r) and period 2π√(r³/GM). [4]
(b) Find the radius of a geostationary orbit, taking its period as 86,164 s. [3]
(c) A satellite in a circular parking orbit 400 km above the surface is to be moved to geostationary orbit by a Hohmann transfer (a half-ellipse with perigee on the parking orbit and apogee on the geostationary orbit). Using conservation of energy and angular momentum, find the speeds at perigee and apogee of the transfer ellipse. [7]
(d) Hence find the two speed increments needed, the total Δv, and the time spent on the transfer ellipse. [6]
markScheme: (a) Gravity provides centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r gives v = √(GM/r); T = 2πr/v = 2π√(r³/GM)
(c) r₁ = 6771 km, r₂ ≈ 42,164 km; r₁v_p = r₂v_a (velocity perpendicular to radius at the apses)
(c) Energy: ½v_p² − GM/r₁ = ½v_a² − GM/r₂, giving v_p = √(2GMr₂/(r₁(r₁ + r₂)))
(c) v_p ≈ 10.07 km/s; v_a = v_p r₁/r₂ ≈ 1.62 km/s
(d) Circular speeds: v₁ = √(GM/r₁) ≈ 7.67 km/s, v₂ = √(GM/r₂) ≈ 3.07 km/s
(d) Δv₁ = v_p − v₁ ≈ 2.40 km/s, Δv₂ = v₂ − v_a ≈ 1.46 km/s; total ≈ 3.86 km/s
(d) a = (r₁ + r₂)/2 ≈ 24,468 km; transfer time = half period = π√(a³/GM) ≈ 1.90 × 10⁴ s ≈ 5.3 hours
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) For a circular orbit the satellite's acceleration is v²/r towards the Earth's centre, supplied by gravity: GMm/r² = mv²/r. So v² = GM/r and v = √(GM/r). The period is the circumference divided by the speed: T = 2πr/v = 2πr√(r/GM) = 2π√(r³/GM).

(b) Rearranging, r³ = GMT²/(4π²) = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ × 86,164² / (4π²) ≈ 7.496 × 10²² m³, so r ≈ 4.216 × 10⁷ m, i.e. about 42,160 km from the Earth's centre (about 35,800 km above the surface).

(c) Parking orbit radius r₁ = 6371 + 400 = 6771 km; target radius r₂ ≈ 42,164 km. At perigee and apogee of the transfer ellipse, the velocity is perpendicular to the radius, so conservation of angular momentum gives r₁v_p = r₂v_a. Conservation of energy per unit mass gives ½v_p² − GM/r₁ = ½v_a² − GM/r₂. Substituting v_a = v_p r₁/r₂: ½v_p²(1 − r₁²/r₂²) = GM(1/r₁ − 1/r₂) = GM(r₂ − r₁)/(r₁r₂). Since 1 − r₁²/r₂² = (r₂ − r₁)(r₂ + r₁)/r₂², this simplifies to v_p² = 2GMr₂ / (r₁(r₁ + r₂)). Numerically, v_p² = 2 × 3.986 × 10¹⁴ × 4.2164 × 10⁷ / (6.771 × 10⁶ × 4.8935 × 10⁷) ≈ 1.0145 × 10⁸, so v_p ≈ 10,070 m/s ≈ 10.07 km/s. Then v_a = v_p r₁/r₂ ≈ 10,072 × 6771/42,164 ≈ 1617 m/s ≈ 1.62 km/s.

(d) Circular speeds: v₁ = √(GM/r₁) = √(3.986 × 10¹⁴/6.771 × 10⁶) ≈ 7673 m/s; v₂ = √(GM/r₂) ≈ 3075 m/s. First burn (at perigee, in the direction of motion): Δv₁ = 10,072 − 7673 ≈ 2399 m/s ≈ 2.40 km/s. Second burn (at apogee, to circularise): Δv₂ = 3075 − 1617 ≈ 1457 m/s ≈ 1.46 km/s. Total Δv ≈ 3.86 km/s. The transfer ellipse has semi-major axis a = (r₁ + r₂)/2 ≈ 2.4468 × 10⁷ m. The satellite travels half the ellipse, taking half its period: t = π√(a³/GM) = π√((2.4468 × 10⁷)³/3.986 × 10¹⁴) ≈ 1.90 × 10⁴ s ≈ 5.3 hours. (Real geostationary transfers also change the orbit's inclination, which is ignored here.)
